props.title: Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters
props.initialSlug: Poetic portrait of a revolutionary writer's last day

sections.content: Paul Schrader's Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters (1985) stands as one of cinema's most ambitious literary biographies, fracturing its narrative into a kaleidoscopic portrait of Japanese author Yukio Mishima. Like Schrader's earlier work on Taxi Driver (1976), the film delves deep into a protagonist's psychological torment. The structure interweaves three distinct visual styles: stark black-and-white biographical scenes, saturated present-day sequences of Mishima's final day, and highly stylized adaptations of his novels. Philip Glass's hypnotic score amplifies the film's operatic intensity, while cinematographer John Bailey creates a visual language as complex as Mishima's own writings.

sections.content: The film's theatrical adaptations of Mishima's novels - "The Temple of the Golden Pavilion," "Kyoko's House," and "Runaway Horses" - represent some of the most striking production design in 1980s cinema. Art director Eiko Ishioka, who later won an Oscar for Bram Stoker's Dracula (1992), creates boldly artificial sets that externalize Mishima's inner world. This approach influenced later biographical films like I'm Not There (2007) and 32 Short Films About Glenn Gould (1993), which similarly fragment their subjects into multiple perspectives.

As a meditation on art, sexuality, and nationalism, Mishima (1985) connects to other films exploring artists' self-destruction, like Naked Lunch (1991) and Love & Diane (2002). The film's exploration of Japanese militarism and masculinity finds echoes in later works like The Sun (2005) about Emperor Hirohito and United Red Army (2007). Schrader's unflinching examination of Mishima's right-wing politics and public suicide makes the film particularly relevant to contemporary discussions about art and extremism. sections.content: While Mishima (1985) was an American production, it connects deeply to the Japanese New Wave cinema of directors like Nagisa Oshima and Shohei Imamura. Like Death by Hanging (1968) and The Ceremony (1971), Schrader's film challenges traditional Japanese values while remaining deeply embedded in Japanese cultural forms. The film's blend of historical drama and avant-garde techniques recalls Hiroshi Teshigahara's Woman in the Dunes (1964), another meditation on identity and confinement.
